extracted.intended_audience: psychiatrists, psychiatric educators, clinical psychiatrists and mental-health policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria for psychiatric theory, clinical practice, training, classification, and integration of biological/psychological/social knowledge — aimed at practicing psychiatrists and those who design psychiatric training and policy. Emphasizes avoiding reductionism and fostering a biopsychosocial, clinically grounded approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive biopsychosocial approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical study and practice need to take into account the biological, the psychological, and the social aspects; a person is a mind-body complex in constant interaction with the environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three aspects are not mutually reducible and are indispensable for understanding and treating the individual patient; a comprehensive, biopsychosocial approach is both practically and theoretically most satisfying and constitutes psychiatry’s hallmark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reductionistic extremes (brainless or mindless psychiatry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychiatry should not swing to either extreme of overemphasizing psychodynamics/social factors (brainless) or overemphasizing biological/neuroscientific factors to the exclusion of subjective experience (mindless).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both extremes threaten psychiatry’s distinct role (risking loss of distinction from neurology or from non-medical counselors). The field must resist fashions that claim single-theory supremacy and instead integrate perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal concern with subjective experience and brain function
rubrics_metrics.description: A psychiatrist’s proper focus includes both subjective experience (the mind) and bodily/brain function; subjective data are legitimate and necessary clinical information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinicians must preserve empathic understanding of the patient’s subjective experience, since the clinician’s interest is in what sheds light on this patient here and now; ignoring subjectivity risks producing 'clinical neuroscience' rather than psychiatry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of clinician role and humanistic values in clinical work
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychiatrists are first and foremost clinicians; clinical practice requires going beyond applied biomedical science to include humanistic, artful reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While scientific knowledge informs care, clinical reasoning must treat each patient as a unique individual; a purely scientific/technological approach can be dangerous unless guided by humanistic values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance general diagnostic principles with individual uniqueness
rubrics_metrics.description: Clinical encounters call for diagnostic reasoning based on general clinical-science principles while also taking into account individual characteristics and subjective experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both kinds of reasoning are required: apply general diagnostic frameworks but adapt them empathically to the unique patient to arrive at a clinically useful understanding and treatment plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification should stimulate research and communication, not be an end in itself
rubrics_metrics.description: A psychiatric classification (e.g., DSM-III) is essential to stimulate testable hypotheses, science, and facilitate communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification is necessary but imperfect; beware 'mania classificatoria' — rigid application can miss disorders or distort clinical care. Classifications should be used to generate research and improve practice, not to constrain it dogmatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate neuroscientific advances but avoid overclaiming applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Neuroscience promises important advances (e.g., in dementia, Alzheimer’s) and should be integrated into psychiatry, but current neuroscientific findings have limited direct applicability and will not obviate the need for a comprehensive approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware the 'Rock' of reductionistic gospel; progress in neuroscience is valuable but should not be proclaimed as replacing biopsychosocial clinical work. Use neuroscientific treatments when they are demonstrably the most effective for the individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select interventions based on likely effectiveness for the patient
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose treatment modalities (biological, psychotherapeutic, social interventions) that are most likely to help the given patient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If physiologic interventions demonstrably achieve desired effects for a patient, they should be welcomed, but not at the expense of dismissing psychotherapy or other approaches when they play an important role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empathic communication and resisting simplistic etiological explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not present simplistic explanations (e.g., 'chemical imbalance') to patients as definitive causes; such explanations can mislead about correlation vs causation and underestimate meaningful psychosocial factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Telling a patient they 'suffer from a chemical imbalance' can be vacuous and may reduce personal agency; clinicians should explain complexity, causal uncertainty, and the role of subjective meaning in illness and recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training psychiatrists with both clinical and neuroscientific competence (liaison/consultation emphasis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Train psychiatrists who retain clinical primacy but are versed in neuroscience and who can function in liaison/consultation roles bridging medicine and psychiatry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Growth of consultation-liaison psychiatry and general hospital psychiatric units exemplifies the need; training should prevent drift away from medicine while fostering collaboration with other medical departments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resist professional dogmatism and politicization of 'science'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid adopting ideological, dogmatic, or politicized positions under the label of 'scientific' that preclude critical inquiry and humane practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples (political dogmatism, overclaiming of psychoanalysis as sole truth) show the danger; maintain open-minded skepticism and require testing/validation of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand testing and validation before wide adoption of new ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: New theoretical or practical approaches should be tested and validated rather than quickly turned into fashions or presented as facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Grinker: accepting ideas as facts without validation is detrimental to an applied science—psychiatry must emphasize empirical testing before broad clinical endorsement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize fluid boundaries of mental disorder
rubrics_metrics.description: Which phenomena count as 'mental disorder' changes over time; the field must acknowledge that boundaries are not fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic committees face social and political pressures around inclusion/exclusion; the fluidity demands humility, ongoing revision, and sensitivity to social context in classification work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against overspecialization; integrate across expanding literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Given exploding scientific publications, psychiatrists must integrate diverse information rather than confining themselves so narrowly that they lose a view of the field as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sponsor development of unified psychopathology frameworks and institutions (e.g., academic chairs, institutes) that foster integration across neuroscience, psychology, and social sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value multiple theoretical perspectives and pursue unification
rubrics_metrics.description: Different approaches (phenomenology, psychoanalysis, experimental brain pathology) each bring factual knowledge and should be held together in attempts at unification (eclecticism that aims for synthesis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eclectic unification is challenging but necessary; each perspective contributes insights that must somehow be assembled to advance psychiatry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain psychiatry’s identity as part of medicine
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychiatry must remain a medical discipline equally concerned with mind and body and resist being usurped by nonmedical mental-health practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Efforts like consultation-liaison psychiatry were intentionally supported to keep psychiatry linked to medicine; retaining medical procedures (diagnosis, integration with general hospitals) is essential to the field’s integrity.
